q: Two heat-summation totals come out identical for a northern site and a southern one, though the northern site enjoys far longer midsummer days. Which index applies a day-length coefficient to correct for that?
opts: The continentality index
The Winkler index
Growing season temperature
The Huglin index
exp: Huglin weights accumulated heat by a latitude coefficient, on the reasoning that a long northern day gives the vine more hours to use the warmth it gets. Winkler counts degree days without any such correction, which is why the two indices rank a German site and a Spanish one differently.

q: Amerine and Winkler summed the daily degrees above ten Celsius from April through October to sort California into bands. What is the resulting quantity called?
exp: Ten degrees is the threshold below which the vine does essentially nothing, so only the warmth above it is counted. The measure is blind to how the heat arrived, which is its weakness: one brutal August week and a long even summer can total the same and ripen fruit quite differently.

q: Rather than a full-year mean, the classification most used in wine climatology today averages temperature over the seven months from April to October in the north. Name that average.
accept: mean temperature of the growing season
average temperature of the growing season
exp: Averaging only the months the vine is awake removes the winter noise that makes annual means useless for comparing regions. The bands it produces, from cool through intermediate and warm to hot, map onto variety suitability far better than latitude does.

q: Two coastal regions share a narrow annual temperature range, yet one bakes dry every summer while the other faces rot pressure at picking. Which variable separates them?
accept: distribution of rainfall through the year
exp: Maritime and Mediterranean climates are both moderate, so temperature alone will not tell them apart. The Mediterranean model puts its rain in the winter and leaves the growing season dry, which is why irrigation and drought are its arguments while the maritime regions argue about fungicide and picking dates.

q: Water changes temperature far more slowly than the land beside it, and that single physical property is the whole of why a coastal vineyard is moderate. Name the property.
accept: high specific heat capacity of water
water has a high specific heat capacity
exp: It takes roughly five times as much energy to warm a mass of water by one degree as it does the same mass of rock, so a large body of water lags the air around it in both directions. That lag is what shortens winters, delays autumn and blunts heat spikes; depth matters more than surface area, which is why a deep lake moderates better than a shallow one of the same size.

q: Tilting the ground toward the sun buys far more energy at fifty degrees of latitude than at thirty. What accounts for the difference?
opts: Days are shorter at high latitude, so each hour of sunshine must do more work
High-latitude air holds more moisture, which traps heat against the slope
The sun sits lower at high latitude, so a slope faces it more squarely
Soils at high latitude are darker and absorb more of the energy reaching them
exp: Energy per square metre depends on the angle at which light strikes the ground, and the closer that angle comes to perpendicular the more of the beam a given patch of ground collects. Near the equator the sun is close to overhead and a slope gains almost nothing, which is why aspect is an obsession on the Mosel and an irrelevance in Mendoza, where elevation does the work instead.

q: Set sunlight aside: the celebrated sites in steep regions still sit on the slope rather than on the flat ground below it. What has gravity done to those two soils over the centuries?
opts: Slopes accumulate a deeper topsoil than the ground below them
Fine material has washed downhill from the slope to the flat
Slopes hold more organic matter, so hillside vines are better fed
Rainfall totals are higher on slopes than on valley floors
exp: Erosion strips clay and organic matter off a gradient and dumps it at the bottom, so the slope keeps a thin, stony, poor profile and the valley floor collects the richness. Poor and thin is what restrains vigour, which is why the hillside is planted and the fertile flat is left to other crops.

q: Vineyards planted within a few degrees of the equator ought to lose all their acidity, and above two thousand metres they do not. Which feature of high tropical sites rescues them?
opts: A short growing season
A very wide diurnal swing
A pronounced winter dormancy
Long summer daylight hours
exp: Thin air at altitude radiates its heat away fast after sunset, so tropical highland sites can run twenty degrees between afternoon and dawn. Nothing else is available to them: there is no winter to enforce dormancy and no seasonal variation in day length at all, so the diurnal swing is doing all of the work.

q: Climbing a hillside costs a vineyard about six-tenths of a degree of mean temperature for every hundred metres gained. Name that rate of cooling with height.
exp: The figure is why elevation substitutes for latitude: three hundred metres up is worth roughly two degrees, which is a large slice of the difference between one growing season band and the next. It is also why altitude is the standard answer to a warming climate in regions that have run out of cooler latitudes to move to.

q: On a still clear night the coldest air in a valley collects on the floor, while the ridge top cools by exposure, leaving a warmer band lying between them. What do growers call that band?
exp: Mid-slope sits above the pooled cold air and below the exposed summit, which is why the oldest vineyards on a hillside are so often in the middle third of it. The belt is a frost-season phenomenon and it moves with the depth of the cold pool, so its lower boundary is worth marking in a bad spring rather than assuming.

q: Dense cold air slides downhill under gravity on a windless night, behaving far more like water than like wind. Meteorology has a name for that downslope flow. Give it.
exp: Because it behaves like a fluid, anything that dams it matters: a solid wall, a dense hedge or an embankment across the bottom of a slope will pond cold air behind it and turn a safe site into a frost trap. The remedy is usually to open a gap rather than to buy machinery.

q: Rainfall on the seaward flank of a coastal range routinely runs to three times the total recorded a short distance inland. Which process concentrates it there?
opts: Convection over warm ground
Orographic lift
A collision of warm and cold fronts
Katabatic drainage
exp: Air forced up over the barrier cools as it expands, passes its dew point and drops its moisture on the windward side. Everything downwind is then working with air that has already been wrung out, which is the whole mechanism behind a rain shadow.

q: A summer marine layer pushes through gaps in a coast range and lies over the vineyards until late morning. What does that fog most directly buy the fruit?
opts: A rise in ultraviolet exposure that thickens the skins
A supply of nitrogen deposited out of the marine air
A cooler, shorter effective day
A measurable increase in growing-season rainfall
exp: The fog caps the temperature and cuts the hours of full sun, so sugar accumulates slowly and acid holds while flavour and tannin catch up. It is a cooling mechanism that works in a region with no rain at all in summer, which is why the coldest sites in California can sit at the latitude of North Africa.

q: Winter survival in Ontario's Niagara Peninsula depends on Lake Ontario, but the moderated air has to be held over the vineyards by a landform standing behind them. Name it.
exp: The escarpment traps lake-warmed air on the bench between rock face and shoreline and sets up a circulation that keeps it moving over the vines. Water alone is not enough this far into a continental winter: without the wall behind it the moderated air would simply drain away inland.

q: Air that has already dumped its moisture climbing the windward slope arrives on the far side warm, dry and gusting, and the Alpine name for that wind is used across the wine world. Give it.
exp: The air warms as it descends and is compressed, and having lost its water on the way up it arrives far drier than it began. Alto Adige and the Valais both bank on it to dry the canopy and finish ripening, and it is the same physics as the Chinook and the Zonda under different names.

q: Moist air moving horizontally over a surface colder than its own dew point produces fog with no overnight cooling of the ground involved at all. Name that class of fog.
exp: Advection fog needs wind to keep the moist air arriving, so it forms and persists in conditions that would blow radiation fog away. That is why coastal fog rolls in during the afternoon and evening while river-valley radiation fog appears at dawn and burns off by mid-morning.
